title: Tabular ML with Honest Evaluation
why: Shows you can frame a prediction problem, avoid data leakage, and report results without fooling yourself. Hiring managers trust engineers who beat a baseline for the right reasons.
brief: Pick a public tabular dataset (for example Adult Income or Telco Churn from OpenML or Kaggle) and build a full scikit-learn pipeline. Compare a dummy baseline, logistic regression, and gradient boosting using a held-out test set and cross-validation, then analyze where the model fails.

milestones.title: Frame the problem and split data
milestones.done: Target, metric, and a stratified train/test split are written down before any modeling; test set is untouched afterwards

milestones.title: Baseline and simple model
milestones.done: DummyClassifier and logistic regression scores are recorded in a results table

milestones.title: Pipeline with cross-validation
milestones.done: Preprocessing lives inside a scikit-learn Pipeline and 5-fold CV mean and std are reported

milestones.title: Stronger model and tuning
milestones.done: Gradient boosting tuned with CV only; test set scored exactly once

milestones.title: Error analysis
milestones.done: Confusion matrix plus at least 3 slices of data where the model does worse, with a written hypothesis for each

milestones.title: Publish
milestones.done: Repo runs end to end from a fresh clone with one command

deliverables: Public GitHub repo with notebook and a reusable train.py
README with problem, metric choice, and results table (baseline vs models)
Error analysis section with plots
Short write-up of what you would do next
rubric: A naive baseline is reported and the final model is compared against it
No preprocessing is fit on test data (pipeline used)
Metric choice is justified for the class balance
Cross-validation mean and spread are reported, not just one score
Error analysis names concrete failure slices
stretch: Add calibration curves and a threshold analysis
Explain predictions with SHAP or permutation importance
Serve the model behind a small FastAPI endpoint
resumeBullet: Built a [model type] classifier on [dataset] with a scikit-learn pipeline and [k]-fold cross-validation, improving [metric] from [baseline value] to [final value] over a naive baseline and documenting [n] failure slices.
pitfalls: Scaling or imputing before the split, which leaks test information
Tuning hyperparameters against the test set
Reporting accuracy on an imbalanced dataset

title: RAG Chatbot Over Your Own Documents
why: RAG is the most common AI application job today. Measuring retrieval and answer quality separately shows you can debug and improve a system instead of guessing.
brief: Build a chatbot that answers questions over a document set you choose (your notes, a docs site, or public PDFs), with chunking, embeddings, vector search, and citations for every answer. Create a small evaluation set and report retrieval and answer quality.
stack: sentence-transformers or a hosted embeddings API
Chroma or MongoDB Atlas Vector Search
Claude API or a local model via Ollama

milestones.title: Ingest and chunk
milestones.done: Documents are parsed and chunked; you have compared at least 2 chunk sizes

milestones.title: Embed and index
milestones.done: All chunks are stored in a vector store and a top-k query returns sensible results for 5 manual tests

milestones.title: Answer with citations
milestones.done: Every answer includes source file and passage references, and refuses when nothing relevant is retrieved

milestones.title: Build the eval set
milestones.done: At least 30 question and expected-source pairs, including some unanswerable questions

milestones.title: Measure and iterate
milestones.done: Hit rate at k and answer quality are reported for at least 2 configurations

milestones.title: Simple UI
milestones.done: Chat page shows answers with clickable citations

deliverables: Public GitHub repo
README with architecture and chunking decisions
Eval set file and results table comparing configurations
Demo video or hosted link
rubric: Retrieval hit rate is measured on at least 30 questions
Answers cite the source passages used
The system declines to answer on out-of-scope questions, tested with examples
At least two configurations are compared with numbers
Eval set is committed and reproducible
stretch: Add hybrid search (BM25 plus vectors) or a reranker and measure the change
Add incremental re-indexing when documents change
resumeBullet: Built a RAG chatbot over [n] documents using [vector store] and [model], raising retrieval hit rate@[k] from [baseline]% to [final]% on a [n]-question eval set and producing cited answers with [x]% judged faithful.
pitfalls: Only testing with a few hand-picked questions and no eval set
Chunks that split tables or sentences so the answer is never retrievable
Not testing questions the documents cannot answer

title: Tool-Using Agent with an MCP Server
why: Shows you can give a model safe, well-specified capabilities and control its behavior. Tool schemas, guardrails, and traces are what separate a real agent from a demo.
brief: Write an MCP server that exposes 3 to 5 tools with JSON schemas for a domain you pick (for example tasks, notes, or a public API), then build an agent loop that calls them. Add error handling, guardrails such as confirmation for write actions and step limits, and record traces of every run.

milestones.title: Design tools
milestones.done: Each tool has a clear description, JSON schema, and validated inputs

milestones.title: Working MCP server
milestones.done: Server runs and its tools can be listed and called from an MCP client such as MCP Inspector

milestones.title: Agent loop
milestones.done: Agent completes a multi-step task by calling at least 2 tools in sequence

milestones.title: Errors and guardrails
milestones.done: Tool failures, bad arguments, and a max-step limit are handled; write actions need confirmation

milestones.title: Traces
milestones.done: Every run saves prompts, tool calls, results, and token usage

milestones.title: Task suite
milestones.done: At least 15 scripted tasks with pass or fail results, including adversarial ones

deliverables: Public GitHub repo
README describing tools, schemas, and guardrails
Sample trace files or screenshots
Task suite results table
rubric: Every tool has a schema and input validation
The loop has a step limit and a tested failure path
Destructive actions are gated
Traces let a reviewer reconstruct each run
Task suite reports success rate including failure cases
stretch: Add an authenticated remote MCP server
Add a second agent or planner and compare success rates
Add prompt injection tests through tool outputs
resumeBullet: Built an MCP server with [n] typed tools and an agent that completes [x]% of [n] benchmark tasks, adding guardrails and tracing that cut [failure type] errors by [y]%.
pitfalls: Vague tool descriptions that cause wrong tool choice
No step limit, so the agent can loop and burn tokens
Trusting tool output as if it were instructions

title: Fine-Tune a Small Open Model with LoRA and Compare to Prompting
why: Shows you understand when fine-tuning helps and when prompting is enough. An honest before and after comparison is rare and valued.
brief: Choose a narrow task (for example structured extraction or classification into a fixed format) and prepare a dataset. Fine-tune a small open model such as Qwen or Llama 3.2 1B/3B with LoRA or QLoRA using Hugging Face PEFT and TRL, then compare it against a well-prompted base model and a hosted model on a held-out set.
stack: Google Colab or Kaggle free GPU

milestones.title: Define task and metric
milestones.done: Task, output format, and automatic metric are written down

milestones.title: Prepare data
milestones.done: Train, validation, and test files exist with no overlap; at least 500 training examples

milestones.title: Prompting baseline
milestones.done: Few-shot prompt score on the test set is recorded

milestones.title: Training run
milestones.done: LoRA or QLoRA run completes and loss curves are saved

milestones.title: Evaluate
milestones.done: Fine-tuned, base, and prompted results are in one table with the same test set

milestones.title: Publish
milestones.done: Adapter and model card are uploaded to Hugging Face Hub

deliverables: Public GitHub repo with training script
Results table: base vs prompted vs fine-tuned
Model card on Hugging Face Hub
Short write-up including cost and time
Sample outputs showing wins and losses
rubric: Test set is never used in training or prompt tuning
A strong prompting baseline is included
Hyperparameters and seed are documented
Failure examples are shown, not only wins
Cost or training time is reported
stretch: Compare LoRA ranks and learning rates
Serve the adapter with vLLM and measure latency
Try preference tuning such as DPO
resumeBullet: Fine-tuned [model] with QLoRA on [n] examples for [task], improving [metric] from [prompted baseline] to [fine-tuned] on a held-out set of [n] while training in [hours] hours on [hardware].
pitfalls: Train and test leakage through duplicate examples
Comparing against a weak, untuned prompt
Judging quality by loss instead of task metrics

title: LLM Evaluation and Observability Harness
why: Evaluation discipline is the top gap in AI teams. This shows you can catch regressions, validate an LLM judge, and control cost.
brief: Build a reusable harness that runs a golden set against an LLM feature (reuse your RAG bot or agent), scores outputs with code checks and an LLM-as-judge, and reports cost and latency. Validate the judge against human labels and run the suite in CI as a regression test.
stack: Claude API or another LLM API

milestones.title: Golden set
milestones.done: At least 50 cases with expected behavior, versioned in the repo

milestones.title: Code-based checks
milestones.done: Format, citation, and keyword checks run without a model

milestones.title: LLM judge
milestones.done: Judge rubric prompt returns structured scores

milestones.title: Judge validation
milestones.done: At least 30 cases hand-labeled by you and judge agreement is reported

milestones.title: Cost and latency
milestones.done: Each run logs tokens, cost, and p50 and p95 latency

milestones.title: CI regression
milestones.done: GitHub Actions fails a pull request when a score drops below a threshold

deliverables: Public GitHub repo with CI badge
README explaining the metrics and thresholds
Judge agreement report with human labels
Sample run report with cost and latency
rubric: Judge agreement with human labels is measured and reported
Golden set has at least 50 cases including edge cases
CI blocks a deliberately introduced regression
Cost and latency are tracked per run
Results are reproducible with fixed settings
stretch: Add pairwise comparison with position swapping
Add a dashboard for run history
resumeBullet: Built an LLM evaluation harness with a [n]-case golden set and an LLM judge reaching [x]% agreement with human labels, running in CI and catching [n] regressions while tracking cost of $[y] per run.
pitfalls: Trusting a judge without checking it against human labels
Golden set too small or too easy to detect change
Ignoring nondeterminism, so CI is flaky

title: Capstone: Production AI Feature in a MERN App
why: Combines your full-stack strength with AI engineering. It shows you can ship an AI feature that is safe, affordable, observable, and measured.
brief: Add an AI feature (for example a RAG assistant or summarizer) to a MERN app with streaming responses over SSE, user auth, rate limiting, per-user cost caps, response caching, and structured logging. Deploy it and document the architecture and eval results in the README.

milestones.title: Core feature
milestones.done: Feature works locally end to end with a defined eval set

milestones.title: Streaming and auth
milestones.done: Tokens stream to the React UI and only logged-in users can call the endpoint

milestones.title: Rate limits and cost caps
milestones.done: Requests are limited per user and a daily token cap returns a clear error

milestones.title: Caching and logging
milestones.done: Repeat requests hit the cache and each call logs user, tokens, cost, and latency

milestones.title: Deploy
milestones.done: App is live on a public URL with secrets in environment variables

milestones.title: Eval and README
milestones.done: Eval results, architecture diagram description, and limits are documented

deliverables: Public GitHub repo
Live demo link
README with architecture diagram description and eval results
Cost and latency numbers
Short write-up of tradeoffs
rubric: Responses stream and handle client disconnects
Auth, rate limiting, and cost caps are each demonstrated
API keys never appear in client code or the repo
README has an architecture description and eval results
Logs allow per-user cost to be computed
stretch: Add fallback to a second model on failure
resumeBullet: Shipped a [feature] in a MERN app with streaming responses, auth, and per-user cost caps, serving [n] requests with p95 latency of [x] s, [y]% cache hit rate, and average cost of $[z] per request.
pitfalls: Calling the LLM API directly from the browser with an exposed key
No cost cap, so one user can exhaust the budget
Shipping without an eval, so quality claims are unsupported
